{"id": "ab4317f5-fbd9-46ca-9842-f2d43086acc1", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "## Making Location A primary, Location B backup

Direct Connect doesn't have an "active/backup" toggle — you influence path selection with BGP attributes on the virtual interfaces at each location. Any of these (not mutually exclusive) will do it:

**For outbound traffic from AWS to your network** (which path AWS uses to reach you):
- **Local preference BGP community tags** — this is the recommended primary method. Tag prefixes advertised from Location A with `7224:7300` (high) and from Location B with `7224:7100` (low). AWS evaluates local preference first, so this wins regardless of path length.
- **AS-PATH prepending** — as a secondary/fallback mechanism, prepend extra AS numbers on the routes advertised from Location B so its path looks longer. Only matters if local preference ties.
- **More specific prefixes** on the active connection also win, independent of the above.

**For inbound traffic to your network from AWS** (which path your network prefers for return traffic):
- Advertise with local preference community tags and/or AS-PATH prepending from your router at Location B so AWS prefers sending to A.
- Advertise a more specific route from Location A.

Order of precedence Direct Connect uses: **most specific prefix → local preference → shortest AS path.** So local preference is the reliable lever; AS-PATH prepending alone can get overridden by prefix specificity or regional distance.

## What to avoid

- **Don't rely on AS-PATH prepending alone if VIFs span different AWS Regions attached to one Direct Connect Gateway.** If VIF-A is in Region 1 and VIF-B is in Region 2, but both reach a VPC in Region 1, AWS will always prefer the same-Region connection regardless of AS-PATH — prepending won't override this. Use local preference community tags instead in this topology.
- **Don't advertise identical prefixes with identical attributes (AS path, MED, community) on both connections** — that creates unintended load-balancing (ECMP) across both paths instead of a real active/passive split, which can cause asymmetric routing and odd troubleshooting if B is meant to be pure backup.
- **Don't mix inconsistent signals** — e.g., tagging local preference high on B while also advertising a more-specific prefix on B. More-specific-prefix wins first, so it'll silently override your local preference intent.
- **Don't forget both directions** — you need to set preference for outbound-from-AWS (community tags on your advertisements) AND for your own router's outbound-to-AWS path selection (your local BGP policy / AS-PATH on what you accept from AWS). Setting only one side gives asymmetric routing.
- **Test failover explicitly** — bring down Location A's connection (or BGP session) and confirm traffic actually shifts to B and back cleanly, rather than assuming the config works.

Want me to check your actual Direct Connect virtual interfaces and BGP configuration in this account to see what's currently advertised at each location?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
